docs.title: Medicaid's January 2027 Double Deadline
docs.text:
An Implementation Guide For Work Requirements And Six-Month Renewals

On January 1, 2027, state Medicaid programs take on two federal mandates at the same time. Adults in the expansion population must demonstrate compliance with a new community engagement requirement, and the same population moves to eligibility renewals every six months. Each change adds verification steps, notices and caseworker decisions to processes that are already stretched. The 2023–24 unwinding showed where that pressure breaks: most coverage losses were procedural, driven by missed documentation rather than ineligibility. For state agencies and their technology partners, readiness depends on systems that verify through existing data, notices members can act on and procedures caseworkers can apply consistently, all in place before the deadline arrives.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
What changed H.R. 1, signed July 4, 2025, made work, study or community service a condition of Medicaid eligibility for many expansion adults, and doubled how often their eligibility is checked.

What breaks Both changes add paperwork, and paperwork is where people actually lose coverage. During the 2023–24 Medicaid unwinding, roughly 24 million people were disenrolled, and between 66% and 74% of those losses were procedural: a missed form or an unanswered notice, not a finding that the person no longer qualified.

What it costs CMS itself projects about 2.3 million coverage losses in 2027 from the new requirement. How many of those come from people who actually meet the rules but can't prove it in time depends largely on how clearly states verify, notify and explain.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
• Ex Parte Renewal - renewing a member's coverage using data the state already holds, without asking the member for anything.
  • Expansion Adults - adults who qualify for Medicaid through the Affordable Care Act's expansion group.
  • Interim Final Rule - a rule that takes effect before the public comment process finishes, and that may later be revised.
  • Look-Back Period - the months before an application that a state checks for compliance.
  • Procedural Disenrollment - losing coverage for a paperwork reason, such as an unreturned form, rather than for being found ineligible.

docs.title: Who It Applies To
docs.text:
Work requirements Non-pregnant adults aged 19 to 64 in the Medicaid expansion group or certain section 1115 demonstrations, who aren't enrolled in or entitled to Medicare. CMS says the rule affects 43 states and D.C.

Six-month renewals Adults covered through Medicaid expansion, whether through the state plan or a waiver covering the whole expansion population. Other groups, such as children, parents and pregnant or postpartum people, keep 12-month renewals, and so do American Indian and Alaska Native enrollees.

docs.title: What Members Must Show
docs.text:
Qualifying activities At least 80 hours a month of work, community service or a work program, or enrollment in education at least half-time. Members can combine activities to reach the total.

Income instead of hours Monthly income of at least the federal minimum wage times 80 hours, which is $580 a month in 2026, also meets the requirement.

When it's checked Applicants must show compliance for one to three consecutive months before the month they apply, with the number of months set by the state. Enrolled members must show at least one compliant month in each eligibility period, and states may check more often.

docs.title: Who Is Exempt
docs.text:
The interim final rule lists categories that states must exclude:

  • Former Foster Youth - who turned 18 on or after January 1, 2023.
  • American Indians And Alaska Natives - regardless of income or activity.
  • Parents And Caregivers - of a child aged 13 or under, or of a person with a disability.
  • Disabled Veterans - with a total disability rating from the VA.
  • Medically Frail Individuals - including people with serious mental illness, substance use disorder, or physical, intellectual or developmental disabilities.
  • Members Already Meeting Other Program Rules - people meeting TANF work requirements, or SNAP household members not subject to SNAP work rules.
  • People In Treatment - in a drug or alcohol treatment and rehabilitation program.
  • Incarcerated Individuals - in a public institution.
  • Pregnant And Postpartum Individuals - through the end of the postpartum period.

States may also offer short-term hardship exceptions for inpatient care, federally declared disasters, travel for medical care, and counties with high unemployment, where unemployment is at least 8% or 1.5 times the national rate, whichever is lower.

docs.title: The Renewal Rules
docs.text:
Automatic renewal first States must try to renew coverage using data they already hold. When the data isn't enough, they send a prepopulated renewal form and give the member at least 30 days to respond.

Two ways to make the switch CMS's State Medicaid Director Letter of March 6, 2026 lets states keep each member's existing renewal date and start six-month periods at the next renewal, or bring renewals forward from January 2027. Bringing them forward can't start before January 1, 2027, can't create a period shorter than six months, and requires a notice to every member whose 12-month period is cut short.

Mixed households Members of one household can now have different renewal cycles. When a six-month renewal turns up information that affects another member, the state must treat it as a change in circumstances.

docs.title: Where The Two Deadlines Collide
docs.text: States that bring renewals forward risk a renewal surge in January 2027, the same month work checks begin. Caseworkers would then face two new processes at once, members would get more notices at once, and CMS has warned that processing backlogs could put a state at risk of compliance action. The safer path, keeping existing renewal dates, spreads that load across the year.

docs.title: What Changes In Eligibility Systems
docs.text:
• Eligibility Rules - new logic for who is subject to the requirement, who is exempt and which months count, applied at application, at renewal and at any extra check the state chooses.
  • Data Matching - automated checks against payroll, claims and agency data, so that members who already comply never receive a request.
  • Notices - new templates for advance outreach, noncompliance, hardship exceptions and coverage loss, each with the timing rules built in.
  • Caseworker Task Queues - work items for cases data can't resolve, sorted by deadline, so the 30-day windows don't lapse unnoticed.
  • Reporting And Audit Trail - a record of every check, notice and decision, since each step can be reviewed at a fair hearing.

docs.title: Documentation Checklist
docs.text:
• Member Notices - written in plain language, telling the member what to do, by when and how, before anything else.
  • Caseworker Procedures - step-by-step guides for exemptions, hardship requests and cases data can't resolve.
  • System Release Notes - a short note for staff with every system change, saying what changed and what they now do differently.
  • Version History - a dated record of every change to notices and procedures, ready for audit and fair hearings.
  • Review Sign-Off - policy, legal and QA review before anything reaches members.

docs.title: Release Notes Template
docs.text: Field What To Write What's Changing One sentence on the change. Who It Affects Members, caseworkers or both. Effective Date The date the change applies. What You Do Now The new steps, numbered. Where To Get Help The contact or resource for questions.

docs.title: Rewriting A Member Notice
docs.text:
An example, written to show the approach. It isn't taken from any state's actual notice.

Before

Pursuant to federal requirements, your continued eligibility for medical assistance is contingent upon verification of compliance with community engagement requirements. Failure to furnish acceptable documentation within the prescribed period may result in termination of benefits.

After

Action needed by [date]: Tell us about your work, school or volunteering

To keep your Medicaid, we need to know you spent at least 80 hours in [month] working, studying, volunteering or in a job program. We couldn't confirm this from the records we have. You can upload pay slips or a school letter at [website], call [number], or return the enclosed form. If something stops you from meeting this requirement, such as a health condition or caring for a child, tell us. You may not need to meet it at all.

docs.title: How States Must Verify
docs.text:
Data before paperwork States must check information they already hold before asking a member for anything. The rule names payroll data, Medicaid claims and encounter data from the past 12 months, records from other state and local agencies, federal data through CMS's data services hub, and the state's own eligibility records.

Self-declaration has a limit For medical frailty, states may accept a member's own statement only through January 2028, and supporting documentation is required at the next renewal.

Health plans can help, but not decide Managed care plans may support outreach and flag members who may be exempt, but they can't make eligibility or compliance decisions.

docs.title: Notices And The 30-Day Window
docs.text:
Advance outreach States must send the first notice at least three months plus the look-back period before the requirement starts. For a January 1, 2027 start, that meant September 1, 2026 for a one-month look-back and July 1, 2026 for a three-month look-back.

Noncompliance notice If the state can't verify compliance, it sends a notice. The member has 30 calendar days to show compliance or an exemption, counted from five days after the date on the notice, and enrolled members keep coverage during that window.

Before coverage ends The state must check whether the person qualifies under another Medicaid pathway, give written notice with fair hearing rights, and explain how losing Medicaid may affect Marketplace premium tax credits.
